ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology Referral — Harriet Tubman

code.originalText: Primary care visit for lifelong headaches and sudden sleep spells

text.paragraph: Lifelong sudden spells and near-daily headaches since a severe head injury in early adolescence, in a 75-year-old woman. Please advise whether the spells are focal seizures or sleep attacks, and on headache prevention. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within two to three weeks. [S]

list.item: Are the spells focal seizures or sleep attacks, and what testing will tell them apart?
Should antiseizure medicine be started now?
Do you agree this is chronic post-traumatic headache with medication overuse, and which non-sedating preventive would you use?
If the spells are sleep attacks, how should her daytime sleepiness be treated without sedating her?

text.paragraph: Since a severe head injury in her early teens she has fallen asleep without warning several times a day, often while seated in conversation or at meetings, waking after a few minutes and picking up where she left off. She has never had weakness with laughter or strong emotion. Headaches on 54 days in the past three months have worsened over the past year despite ibuprofen most days; ibuprofen was stopped today, with acetaminophen limited to 2 days a week and a headache diary. Blood pressure 146/86 mmHg. PROMIS sleep-related impairment T-score 68. Sodium, potassium, creatinine, glucose, hemoglobin, ferritin, TSH, and vitamin B12 are normal. MoCA 26; PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PC-PTSD-5 are below their thresholds. She does not drive and does not want medicine that makes her duller [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Harriet Tubman was born into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in early 1822 by the National Park Service account, and was named Araminta, or Minty, by her parents, Ben and Rit Ross; she was the fifth of nine children. [D]
Her birth year is uncertain: the Dictionary of Canadian Biography gives 1820 or 1821, while the National Park Service and the Maryland State Archives give about 1822. [D]

Hired out from the age of six, Tubman was struck in the head in her early teens, about age 13 in the mid-1830s, by an iron weight an overseer threw at another enslaved person at a village store; she was nearly killed, received little or no medical care, and was affected by the injury for the rest of her life. [D]

After the injury Tubman had headaches and sudden spells of sleep that came on even in the middle of work or conversation, at frequent intervals, and ended abruptly after a few minutes, along with vivid dreams and visions; contemporaries described the spells into her old age. [D]
Historians have proposed that the injury caused temporal lobe epilepsy, citing dreamlike trances in which she appeared conscious. [R]

A 2023 review argued that temporal lobe epilepsy is unlikely, because she could be roused and no auras, automatisms, or post-ictal confusion were described, and proposed post-traumatic narcolepsy instead, while concluding that no definitive explanation is possible. [R]

In her later years Tubman said that a Boston surgeon had opened her skull to relieve her headaches; historians place the operation in the late 1890s at Massachusetts General Hospital, but no record of it has been found. [D]

Tubman married John Tubman in 1844, escaped to Philadelphia in 1849, guided about 70 people to freedom by 1860, served the Union army in South Carolina as a nurse, scout, and spy, and settled in Auburn, New York, where she married Nelson Davis in 1869. [D]

list.item: Chronic post-traumatic headache since an adolescent head injury: active, confirmed [S]
Sequelae of a traumatic brain injury in adolescence, a skull fracture by historical account: active, confirmed [S]

Obtain a routine EEG and brain MRI, then capture typical spells on ambulatory EEG with video; start antiseizure medicine only if the spells prove epileptic. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults (Krumholz A, et al. Neurology 2015;84(16):1705-1713) (2015) [S]

Overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test to evaluate excessive daytime sleepiness. Guideline: Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (Maski K, et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(9):1881-1893) (2021) [S]

Start modafinil 100 mg each morning with two scheduled 15-minute naps a day; check blood pressure and heart rate at follow-up. Guideline: Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (Maski K, et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(9):1881-1893) (2021) [S]

Stop daily ibuprofen, limit acute treatment to 2 days a week, and keep a headache diary. Guideline: The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (Cephalalgia 2018;38(1):1-211) (2018); The American Headache Society Consensus Statement: Update on integrating new migraine treatments into clinical practice (Ailani J, et al. Headache 2021;61(7):1021-1039) (2021) [S]

Start non-sedating headache prevention with candesartan, titrated after a potassium and creatinine check. Guideline: The American Headache Society Consensus Statement: Update on integrating new migraine treatments into clinical practice (Ailani J, et al. Headache 2021;61(7):1021-1039) (2021) [S]

Screen mood, anxiety, trauma symptoms, and cognition at baseline with a trauma-informed approach, and repeat the PHQ-9 at follow-up. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults (Krumholz A, et al. Neurology 2015;84(16):1705-1713) (2015); Treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (Maski K, et al. J Clin Sleep Med 2021;17(9):1881-1893) (2021) [S]
